---
title: "Quiz: SVMs for pixel classification"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. The pixel classifier of the random forests day: paint strokes, compute a feature stack, train, look, correct; here with an SVM.

---

**Q1.** Why does an RBF SVM need standardised features while a random forest does not?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does each method compute with the feature values?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The RBF kernel function depends on the **distance** between feature vectors, which is dominated by the features with the largest numbers; features with small ranges become invisible. A forest only compares one feature at a time with a threshold, and a threshold works the same in any units.
:::

---

**Q2.** You standardise with the mean and standard deviation of **all** pixels of the image, including the held-out region you evaluate on. What is wrong with that?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which data may influence the model?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The held-out pixels then influence the model (through $\mu_j$, $s_j$): information leaks from the evaluation data into training, and the measured error can be optimistic. Compute the statistics on the training pixels (in cross-validation: on the training folds) and apply them unchanged to everything else.
:::

---

**Q3.** Cross-validation with folds by pixel reports 0% error; with folds by stroke 19%. Which do you report, and why do they differ?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where are the neighbours of a held-out pixel?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
By stroke. With folds by pixel, each held-out pixel's neighbours (nearly identical, from the same stroke) are in training, so even memorising gets it right. With folds by stroke the held-out pixels come from strokes the SVM has not seen, as new parts of the image will be.
:::

---

**Q4.** A cross-validation map over $(C, \gamma)$ is worst in the corner with the largest $C$ and $\gamma$. Explain.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Unit 3: what does an RBF SVM with large $\gamma$ and large $C$ do to the training points?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Large $\gamma$: each bump covers only its own training pixel; large $C$: no violation is tolerated. The SVM builds an island around every training pixel and calls everything else by the default value $b$: it memorises (zero training error) and fails on held-out strokes. Overfitting.
:::

---

**Q5.** A one-vs-rest SVM gives a pixel $f_1 = -0.5$, $f_2 = -0.2$, $f_3 = -0.9$. Which class, and how sure is it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many classifiers claim the pixel?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Class 2 (the largest $f$), but none of the three SVMs claims the pixel: it lies in a region that each SVM assigns to "the rest". The decision compares uncalibrated values and is unreliable; the pixel is a good place to paint.
:::

---

**Q6.** How many SVMs does one-vs-one train for 4 classes? And one-vs-rest?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One per pair; one per class.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
One-vs-one: $4 \cdot 3/2 = 6$. One-vs-rest: 4.
:::

---

**Q7.** Nuclei are only 5% of the painted pixels and the SVM misses many of them. Name two remedies that do not need more painting.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One changes the training, one the decision.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Class weights: a larger penalty $C$ for nucleus violations (e.g. balancing weights $n/(k\,n_c)$). Or keep the SVM and lower the threshold on $f$ for the nucleus class, trading precision for recall (an ROC curve shows the trade-off).
:::

---

**Q8.** When would you choose an SVM over a random forest for pixels, and when a neural network?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many labels, and where do the features come from?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
An SVM: few labelled pixels and a good hand-made feature stack, when you are willing to standardise and cross-validate $(C, \gamma)$; it is about as accurate as a forest there, but slower to predict and more work to tune. A neural network: many labelled images, when the features themselves should be learnt (the neural networks day). The forest remains the low-effort baseline.
:::
